Oscar Munanura New Chief of Uganda’s Defence Intelligence Uvira City Could Fall Anytime, FRN Rebels 8Kms Away Socials EBOLA in Focus Kenya’s 5000 Health Workers to Get Zaire Ebola Virus Vaccine Jab By Bigabo Last updated: October 24, 2026 Share 2 Min Read SHARE More than 5, 000 health workers and other Frontline responders in Kenya are scheduled to get immunised with Zaire Ebola virus Vaccine. According to emerging reports, the government of Kenya has requested for over 10,000 vaccine doses from the World Health Organisation. The request forms part of efforts to strengthen protection for frontline personnel involved in surveillance, patient care and outbreak response. Patrick Amoth the Health Director-General said authorities hope the vaccine could offer cross-protection against the Bundibugyo strain due to similarities between the viruses. Dr. Patrick, the Director General in Kenya’s Ministry of Health (MoH) The Zaire Ebola vaccine is designed to protect against the Zaire species of the Ebola virus, while its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo species has not been established. The anticipated cross-protection therefore remains a possibility requiring scientific evidence. Ebola in Kenya Kenya confirmed an outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo Ebola virus, with 10 total cases and 2 deaths reported as of late October 2026. According to details the first case was of a Kenyan man who traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) through Uganda and arrived in Nairobi on October 3th He passed away on October 5th. news.content_title: Large-scale meteorological patterns linked to Ebola virus outbreaks
news.content: A study led by the University of Malaga has shown that outbreaks of Ebola virus do not occur randomly over time; rather, their appearance is linked to specific large-scale meteorological patterns, even with oscillations occurring in regions thousands of miles away from Central Africa, where they are currently suffering from an epidemic of this disease, which can be fatal. The scientific team, which also includes the Spanish Institute of Oceanography, the Manchester Metropolitan University and the Center for International Forestry Research, calls these links "teleconnections" and advocates their analysis as a "clue" to predict where and when the risk of Ebola increases. According to the latest report from the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, based on data collected through September 26, more than 8,000 confirmed infections have been recorded in the latest outbreak, which began in May, including 3,901 deaths, with a case fatality rate of nearly 50 percent. This new finding, obtained after collecting data on 49 outbreaks in Africa between 1976 and 2025 and comparing them in a database with 26 climate oscillation indices, could be used as a means of epidemiological surveillance, capable of detecting early warning signals to identify periods and regions where weather conditions may be more favorable for the occurrence of new outbreaks. The paper has been published in the scientific journal Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment , from the prestigious publisher Springer Nature. From the Pacific to Africa: following a climatic track The scientists used this data until 2018 to build the models and dedicated the years 2019-2025 to seeing if they could forecast new outbreaks. They identified four climatic oscillation indices that were particularly associated with the distribution of outbreaks: the Caribbean Sea Surface Temperature Index (CAR) - no longer available since February 2020 - , the Dipole Mode Index (IMD), the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO) and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), the latter being the most frequent indicator or "signal" and, therefore, the most important macroclimatic factor of the model. Our proposed interpretation is that these large oscillations modify meteorological patterns, for example, precipitation in the African continent, and these can alter ecological conditions that favor the occurrence of outbreaks." Raimundo Real, one of the authors of the paper, Zoology professor, UMA In this sense, the Biogeography and Macroecology professor also at the University of Malaga Jesús Olivero, another of the authors of the paper, clarifies that this does not mean that these distant climate indicators directly cause Ebola, but they may serve as an early warning "clue" of environmental conditions more closely linked to the biological phenomenon. "Early warning systems are essential for combating infectious diseases. To achieve this, it is not enough to detect cases of the disease early; we must anticipate them by monitoring risk factors, and our predictive tool could be key to this effort," adds Olivero. Surveillance tool The researchers estimate that the "useful window" of these large climatic oscillations would be six to twelve months before a potential event, so their predictive capacity is still limited and further research along these lines would be needed before they could be considered an autonomous predictive system. Nevertheless, the study represents an initial step as a surveillance tool that could help activate preparedness measures when climate conditions indicate an increased risk, identifying periods and locations that warrant closer epidemiological monitoring. The study of the biogeography of Central African wildlife This scientific team of the UMA, which includes researchers from the Faculty of Sciences Miguel ángel Farfán and Ana L. Márquez, has been working for more than a decade on the study of the distribution of the Ebola virus in Africa, seeking to gain a better understanding of the transmission mechanisms of this disease, as well as on the analysis of the occurrence of new outbreaks. Ebola is a zoonosis, that is, a disease transmitted from animals to humans. When the 2014 epidemic occurred, these researchers at the UMA had already been studying the biogeography of Central African wildlife for some time, as well as the human interaction with wildlife through hunting. "Since this same wildlife is part of the zoonotic cycle of Ebola, we decided to apply what we had learned to the study of this disease, and we discovered that we had a lot to contribute," they explain. This last project provides a new perspective on how outbreaks of infectious diseases do not depend on a single factor: the interaction between climate, ecosystems, species distribution, and local conditions can generate "temporary windows" during which an outbreak is more likely to occur. "Identifying these windows in advance could give healthcare systems additional time to prepare. Our goal is to build an 'observatory' capable of generating updated risk forecasts based on wildlife, deforestation, macroclimate, and local weather conditions", they conclude. The study is part of the project "Patogeografía espacio-temporal de las zoonosis mediadas por vertebrados voladores" [Spatial-temporal pathogeography of zoonoses mediated by flying vertebrates], co-financed by the European Regional Development Funds (ERDF) and managed by the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation and in the PPRO-RNM262-G-2023 project of the University of Malaga, financed by the Regional Government of Andalusia and the ERDF. It has also received support from the Center for International Forestry Research (CIFOR) through a Transfer of Research Results Contract. Source: Journal reference: Real, R., et al. (2026). Ebola-virus outbreaks are teleconnected with macroclimatic oscillations. Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment . DOI: 10.1007/s00477-026-03365-1. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00477-026-03365-1

Márquez, has been working for more than a decade on the study of the distribution of the Ebola virus in Africa, seeking to gain a better understanding of the transmission mechanisms of this disease, as well as on the analysis of the occurrence of new outbreaks. Ebola is a zoonosis, that is, a disease transmitted from animals to humans. When the 2014 epidemic occurred, these researchers at the UMA had already been studying the biogeography of Central African wildlife for some time, as well as the human interaction with wildlife through hunting. "Since this same wildlife is part of the zoonotic cycle of Ebola, we decided to apply what we had learned to the study of this disease, and we discovered that we had a lot to contribute," they explain. This last project provides a new perspective on how outbreaks of infectious diseases do not depend on a single factor: the interaction between climate, ecosystems, species distribution, and local conditions can generate "temporary windows" during which an outbreak is more likely to occur. "Identifying these windows in advance could give healthcare systems additional time to prepare. Our goal is to build an 'observatory' capable of generating updated risk forecasts based on wildlife, deforestation, macroclimate, and local weather conditions", they conclude. The study is part of the project "Patogeografía espacio-temporal de las zoonosis mediadas por vertebrados voladores" [Spatial-temporal pathogeography of zoonoses mediated by flying vertebrates], co-financed by the European Regional Development Funds (ERDF) and managed by the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation and in the PPRO-RNM262-G-2023 project of the University of Malaga, financed by the Regional Government of Andalusia and the ERDF. It has also received support from the Center for International Forestry Research (CIFOR) through a Transfer of Research Results Contract. Source: Journal reference: Real, R., et al. (2026). news.content: Skip to main content Global Issues Social, Political, Economic and Environmental Issues That Affect Us All Search this siteSearch Get free updates via Email Web/RSS Feed Facebook Twitter Main menu: Menu Home About Issues World News Support Contact You are here: Home News 2026 October Kenya: 20 Ebola contacts released from quarantine Kenya: 20 Ebola contacts released from quarantine © WHO/Genna Print Healthcare workers in Kenya prepare to deal with cases of Ebola. Tuesday, October 27, 2026 UN News Twenty people associated with Kenya’s first case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease have been reunited with their families after being released from quarantine following completion of the mandatory 21-day monitoring period. The contacts were discharged on Monday, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO), which has been assisting the Kenyan authorities with Ebola preparedness since the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak on 15 May. Another 98 contacts remain in quarantine. No risk to the community The people who are now back at home remained asymptomatic during quarantine and underwent standard protocols, including a final health assessment, counselling on post-discharge precautions and follow-up where required before being released. “We ask communities to welcome them home warmly,” said Dr Patrick Amoth, Kenya’s director general for health. “Having completed 21 days without symptoms, they pose no risk of infection to anyone.” The WHO representative to Kenya, Dr Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo, echoed his message. “People who complete quarantine have helped protect their families, their communities and the whole country,” she said. Rush to trace contacts Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case on 6 October – a Kenyan man who had been working in the DRC, where infections and deaths continue to mount. He flew back to Kenya via Uganda on 3 October and died in a Nairobi hospital two days later. The Ministry of Health conducted robust contact tracing of anyone who may have been exposed, including family members, airline passengers and crew, airport workers and medical personnel. By 22 October, all contacts were traced – both in Kenya and abroad – and placed in quarantine. As of Monday, eight contacts had developed symptoms and were confirmed positive for Ebola disease through laboratory testing. They were immediately transferred to the Ebola treatment centre in Nairobi. Praise and support In total, Kenya has reported nine confirmed Ebola cases and two deaths. All are part of one connected group and there is no evidence that the virus has spread to the community. “WHO commends the Ministry of Health, the Kenya National Public Health Institute, national and county health teams for their work in responding quickly to every new case,” said Dr. Kimambo. The UN agency continues to support Kenya in all aspects of Ebola response, including coordination, disease surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory testing, case management, infection prevention and control, health screening at points of entry, risk communication and community engagement. Although there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo virus disease, WHO stressed that early detection and supportive care improve chances of recovery. © UN News (2026) — All Rights Reserved. These contacts remained asymptomatic and underwent standard protocols, including health assessments and follow-up, before being discharged. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been assisting Kenya since the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak on May 15, 2026. As of the release, Kenya has reported nine confirmed Ebola cases and two deaths, all part of a single connected group. No community spread was observed, and WHO emphasized that early detection and supportive care improve recovery chances. Facebook Twitter Print Email Ebola: 20 contacts released from quarantine in Kenya, amid vaccine ‘hope’ in DR Congo 27 October 2026 Health Twenty people associated with Kenya’s first case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease have been reunited with their families after being released from quarantine following completion of a mandatory 21-day monitoring period. They were discharged on Monday, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO), which has been assisting the Kenyan authorities with Ebola preparedness since the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak on 15 May. Another 98 contacts remain in quarantine. No risk to the community The people who are now back at home remained asymptomatic during quarantine and underwent standard protocols, including a final health assessment, counselling on post-discharge precautions and follow-up where required before being released. “We ask communities to welcome them home warmly,” said Dr Patrick Amoth, Kenya’s director general for health. “Having completed 21 days without symptoms, they pose no risk of infection to anyone.” The WHO representative to Kenya, Dr Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo, echoed his message. “People who complete quarantine have helped protect their families, their communities and the whole country,” she said. Rush to trace contacts Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case on 6 October – a Kenyan man who had been working in the DRC, where the caseload is approaching the 10,000 mark. He flew back to Kenya via Uganda on 3 October and died in a Nairobi hospital two days later. The Ministry of Health conducted robust contact tracing of anyone who may have been exposed, including family members, airline passengers and crew, airport workers and medical personnel. By 22 October, all contacts were traced – both in Kenya and abroad – and placed in quarantine. As of Monday, eight contacts had developed symptoms and were confirmed positive for Ebola disease through laboratory testing. They were immediately transferred to the Ebola treatment centre in Nairobi. Praise and support In total, Kenya has reported nine confirmed Ebola cases and two deaths. All are part of one connected group and there is no evidence that the virus has spread to the community. “WHO commends the Ministry of Health, the Kenya National Public Health Institute, national and county health teams for their work in responding quickly to every new case,” said Dr. Kimambo. The UN agency continues to support Kenya in all aspects of Ebola response, including coordination, disease surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory testing, case management, infection prevention and control, health screening at points of entry, risk communication and community engagement. Although there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo virus disease, WHO stressed that early detection and supportive care improve chances of recovery. DRC vaccine trial Meanwhile, “a crucial clinical trial” was launched in the DRC on Friday to determine if vaccines can provide protection against the disease, said WHO’s Dr. Meg Doherty, speaking from the eastern city of Bunia to journalists in Geneva. The TUMAINI trial platform is designed so that several vaccine candidates can be evaluated within one research framework using a strategy called the ring vaccination approach involving contacts of people with a confirmed case of Ebola. “Tumaini actually means ‘hope’ in Swahili, and is giving us some hope,” said Dr. Doherty, director of WHO’s Department of Science for Health. Soundcloud A moving experience The first vaccine under evaluation is Ervebo which has been effective against Ebola caused by the Zaire virus. It is not yet known if it will have any protective effect against the Bundibugyo strain. Dr. Doherty attended the launch, where four people were vaccinated. “It was moving to see this trial begin, just as it has been deeply sad to see the effect of this outbreak on communities,” she said. “I lived and worked in DRC nearly 40 years ago, and it is quite heartbreaking to see this beautiful country challenged by outbreaks on top of humanitarian crises.” Evaluations and recommendations Last week, WHO convened technical advisory groups that evaluated the evidence on two vaccines designed specifically against Bundibugyo virus: ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and mRNA-1469 developed by the American company Moderna. Recommendations will be published this week. “In the meantime, rings are being set up, with people who have a family member sick with Ebola, or who have been exposed to the virus another way,” she said, noting that two rings are currently in place and several more are being prepared. “Community members are already walking into the site asking to be enrolled, highlighting the intense need for an efficacious vaccine,” she added. ‘An important step’ Dr. Doherty explained that a decade ago, WHO and partners used the ring vaccination approach in Guinea during the West African Ebola outbreak to help establish the efficacy of the Ervebo vaccine. “Today, scientists are building on that experience to seek answers about the Bundibugyo virus,” she said. The trial is led by the Congolese authorities and is integrated into the ongoing response to the outbreak. It is being managed by the National Public Health and Biomedical Research Institute, known by the French acronym IRNRB. “We do not yet know for certain when results will begin to emerge. We expect it will take several months,” she said. “But already, having this trial in place is an important step towards gathering scientific data that will help policy makers reach decisions on vaccine use, and we anticipate, to protect people in this outbreak and future outbreaks.” Dr Doherty noted that several other vaccines are under development, “and as they go through their initial studies, if they look promising, they too could be brought into this vaccine platform trial.” Ebola Virus Disease Facebook Twitter Print Email Back to top

analysis.brief_en: In Kenya, 20 individuals associated with the country’s first case of Bundibugyo virus disease were released from quarantine on 27 October 2026 after completing a 21-day monitoring period. These contacts remained asymptomatic and underwent health assessments, counseling, and follow-up before being discharged. Kenya confirmed its first case on 6 October 2026, involving a man who returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and later died in a Nairobi hospital. The Ministry of Health traced all contacts, including those abroad, by 22 October 2026. Eight contacts developed symptoms and tested positive for Ebola disease, but no community spread was reported. The WHO commended Kenya’s health response and continues to support the country in surveillance, testing, and risk communication. Meanwhile, the DRC is conducting a vaccine trial for Bundibugyo virus disease, with the TUMAINI platform evaluating multiple vaccine candidates. The trial, named after the Swahili word for 'hope,' aims to assess vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain, though results are not yet available. The WHO also highlighted the importance of early detection and supportive care in improving recovery chances, as no licensed vaccine or treatment exists for Bundibugyo virus disease.

news.title_zh: 埃博拉:20名接触者在肯尼亚被解除隔离,刚果民主共和国充满“希望” - 联合国新闻
news.source_body_en: In Kenya, 20 individuals associated with the country’s first case of Bundibugyo virus disease were released from quarantine on 27 October 2026 after completing a 21-day monitoring period. These contacts remained asymptomatic and underwent health assessments, counseling, and follow-up before being discharged. Kenya confirmed its first case on 6 October 2026, involving a man who returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and later died in a Nairobi hospital. The Ministry of Health traced all contacts, including those abroad, by 22 October 2026. Eight contacts developed symptoms and tested positive for Ebola disease, but no community spread was reported. The WHO commended Kenya’s health response and continues to support the country in surveillance, testing, and risk communication. Meanwhile, the DRC is conducting a vaccine trial for Bundibugyo virus disease, with the TUMAINI platform evaluating multiple vaccine candidates. The trial, named after the Swahili word for 'hope,' aims to assess vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain, though results are not yet available. The WHO also highlighted the importance of early detection and supportive care in improving recovery chances, as no licensed vaccine or treatment exists for Bundibugyo virus disease.
news.content_zh: 在肯尼亚,与该国首例本迪布焦病毒病相关的 20 名人员在完成 21 天的监测期后于 2026 年 10 月 27 日解除隔离。这些接触者仍然没有症状,并在出院前接受了健康评估、咨询和随访。肯尼亚于 2026 年 10 月 6 日确认了第一例病例,涉及一名从刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 返回的男子,后来在内罗毕一家医院死亡。卫生部截至 2026 年 10 月 22 日追踪了所有接触者,包括国外接触者。八名接触者出现症状,埃博拉病毒检测呈阳性,但没有社区传播的报告。世界卫生组织赞扬肯尼亚的卫生应对措施,并将继续在 监测、检测和风险沟通方面支持该国。与此同时,刚果民主共和国正在开展针对 Bundibugyo 病毒病的 疫苗 试验,TUMANI 平台评估多个 疫苗 候选药物。该试验以斯瓦希里语中的“希望”一词命名,旨在评估 疫苗 对 Bundibugyo 菌株的功效,但结果尚未公布。世卫组织还强调了早期检测和支持性护理对于提高康复机会的重要性,因为尚无针对本迪布焦病毒病的许可 疫苗 或 治疗。

OffOn Stream on 1st person inoculated in trial for Ebola vaccine to protect against strain behind DRC outbreak The trial will test multiple vaccine candidates. ByMary Kekatos October 27, 2026, 8:44 PM Share The first person has been inoculated in a clinical trial for a vaccine that could help protect against the viral strain behind the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders). Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV), a rare variant of Ebola, is behind the DRC outbreak that has led to more than 10,000 cases and nearly 5,000 deaths, the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa posted Tuesday. There are no currently no vaccines or treatments available to treat Bundibugyo virus. The Tumaini clinical trial, as it's known, is evaluating the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity -- meaning the ability to generate an immune response -- of several vaccine candidates. A health worker collects a blood sample from a patient before administering a dose of the Tumaini vaccine against Ebola virus, in Ituri, Congo, Oct. 23, 2026. Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo Related What we know about the spread of Ebola amid growing outbreak in DRC The trial is being co-sponsored and co-led by the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in the DRC and the University of Antwerp's Global Health Institute in Belgium. Partners include the Congo Ministry of Health, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the World Health Organization, and the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. Participants are made up of people who at the time of enrollment were contacts within the previous 21 days of a patient who is a newly confirmed case of Bundibugyo virus disease, according to a summary of the clinical trial posted on the National Institutes of Health website. A healthcare worker in protective clothing is disinfected by a colleague inside a treatment center for Ebola patients in Beni, North Kivu province, eastern Congo, Sept. 26, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo On day 1 of the trial, participants are randomized to receive either a BDBV vaccine candidate or standard treatment, according to the clinical trial summary. On day 29, all participants receive the alternative intervention so that every participant is offered a candidate vaccine while allowing the comparison between groups to remain blinded. Popular Reads Dollar General sued by FTC, 20 states for what's being described as deceptive pricing 1 day ago Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after basketball game altercation Oct 23 Judge rules Trump DOJ 'unlawfully' fired Maurene Comey 1 day ago An independent data monitoring committee will review data accumulated during the trial while additional vaccine candidates are added to the evaluation and others are discontinued if they are shown to be ineffective. "The overall aim is to generate robust evidence to support the use of BDBV vaccines for outbreak response and future epidemic preparedness," the summary states. Related Nigerian medical groups call for nationwide measures after 1st Ebola case MSF said Monday that the first vaccine candidate being studied is ERVEBO, which was developed and licensed to protect against the Zaire ebolavirus, which is the deadliest Ebola strain. At least two Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates being developed by Moderna and the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, and funded by CEPI, will be tested, according to MSF, which also said the Tumaini trial will notably include children. "Children are among those hardest hit by the Ebola outbreak in certain regions, yet they have historically been underrepresented in clinical research," said Valérie Briand, head of MSF's research division, Epicentre. "The inclusion of pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, as well as children from one year of age for the ERVEBO vaccine, represents an important step toward generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials." See latest updates Ebola: First person vaccinated in Tumaini clinical trial The Tumaini clinical trial aims to evaluate the safety and efficacy of vaccine candidates specific to Bundibugyo virus, which is driving the current Ebola outbreak in DR Congo. October 26, 2026 Share Share in FacebookShare in BlueSkyShare in LinkedInShare in TwitterShare in Mail A team member at MSF's Ebola treatment center near Kitatumba Hospital in Butembo, North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Lucie Ringué/MSF Related Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola Vaccination Outbreaks and epidemics View more Related Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola Vaccination Outbreaks and epidemics View more The first participant in the Tumaini clinical trial of vaccine candidates against Bundibugyo virus, which causes Ebola disease, was vaccinated today, as the outbreak continues in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and its research arm, Epicentre, are among several partners involved in this trial, which takes place in Bunia, Ituri province — the early epicenter of the outbreak. DRC is facing the largest Bundibugyo outbreak ever recorded, and the second-largest Ebola disease outbreak to date. There is currently no approved vaccine against Bundibugyo, which is one of several viruses causing Ebola disease. The Tumaini Phase 2/3 clinical trial aims to close that gap by evaluating the safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of vaccine candidates. One of the candidates, ERVEBO, was developed and licensed to protect against the Zaire ebolavirus — not Bundibugyo, which is the virus driving the current outbreak. Marie Sembu, a nurse with the Congolese Ministry of Health, fills out an ERVEBO vaccination card for Dr. Anne Mushiya during the launch of the BRAVO clinical trial in Bunia. | DR Congo 2026 © Kristen Poels/MSF Trial is a critical step in the ongoing Ebola response “The Tumaini trial represents a critical step toward addressing the urgent needs of people most affected by Bundibugyo virus,” said MSF medical director Dr. Bern-Thomas Nyang'wa. “MSF brings to this trial its experience doing clinical research in close collaboration with affected communities. Working in partnership with communities is essential for building trust and ensuring meaningful participation in the development of vaccines that are effective, adapted, and accessible to those who need them most.” Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities, and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks. The trial is co-led and co-sponsored by the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale and the University of Antwerp’s Global Health Institute. Other partners involved include the Congolese Ministry of Health, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, Africa CDC, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the Institute of Tropical Medicine. Working in partnership with communities is essential for building trust and ensuring meaningful participation in the development of vaccines that are effective, adapted, and accessible to those who need them most. Dr. Bern-Thomas Nyang'wa, MSF physician This clinical trial allows several vaccine candidates to be evaluated simultaneously, which can help shorten the time it takes to determine whether a vaccine is effective and can potentially be approved for wider use. Vaccines will be administered through a ring vaccination approach, which focuses on people who have had contact with someone with Ebola and those at highest risk of infection. Technical details about Tumaini are available on ClinicalTrials.gov under the trial number NCT07842107. Vaccine candidates are selected through an independent prioritization process led by WHO’s Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization, and corresponding protocol amendments are approved by ACOREP, the national regulatory authority. The first candidate being used in the trial is ERVEBO. Preparations are underway for two Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI)-funded Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates that are being developed by Moderna and the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India. Furaha, age 3, prepares to return home after recovering from Ebola disease at MSF's Ebola treatment center in Mongbwalu, Ituri province. | DR Congo 2026 © Alexis Huguet/MSF Including children in Ebola research and development Tumaini, which means “hope” in Swahili, also represents an important step toward protecting children. While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, children face the highest risk of death, yet they are often excluded from related clinical research or included only after significant delays. This means they often get access to medical tools far too late, if at all. The Tumaini trial notably includes children. “Children are among those hardest hit by the Ebola outbreak in certain regions, yet they have historically been underrepresented in clinical research,” said Valérie Briand, head of the research department at MSF’s Epicentre. “The inclusion of pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, as well as children from one year of age for the ERVEBO vaccine, represents an important step toward generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials. Discussions are ongoing to extend the inclusion of younger children for specific vaccine candidates.” The Tumaini trial complements other ongoing vaccine trials and studies, including BRAVO, which MSF is also involved in and which focuses solely on determining the efficacy of ERVEBO against Bundibugyo. news.content: News Technology Business Entertainment Science & Health Knowledge Base Font ResizerAa Search News Technology Business Entertainment Science & Health Knowledge Base Follow US Tumaini Trial Begins Vaccinating Participants in DR Congo Last updated: October 25, 2026 12:36 am By Pam Belluck Science & Health 7 Min Read SHARE First participants in the Tumaini vaccine trial have reportedly been vaccinated in Bunia, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province, opening a study meant to answer a still-unresolved question: whether an existing Ebola vaccine can protect people against Bundibugyo virus disease. Several reports published Oct. 24 said the first volunteers received Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. The launch, reported by Al Jazeera and corroborated by MedicalXpress in an AFP report, is a research milestone during an active outbreak, not evidence that the vaccine works against Bundibugyo virus. No safety, immune-response or efficacy results from Tumaini have been released. Table of Contents Why Ervebo is being studied How Tumaini is designed to work A vaccine study, separate from the treatment trial What evidence the trial could provide Why Ervebo is being studied Bundibugyo virus is distinct from Zaire ebolavirus, even though both are among the viruses that can cause Ebola disease. A vaccine’s protection against one virus cannot be assumed to extend to another; cross-protection has to be demonstrated in study results. In May, a World Health Organization expert review said no vaccine or treatment had been specifically approved for Bundibugyo virus disease. It described the evidence that Ervebo might protect against Bundibugyo virus as limited and inconclusive, and advised that its use for that purpose be evaluated in carefully designed research. That is the purpose of Tumaini, whose name means “hope” in Swahili. The trial is not a routine outbreak vaccination campaign. It is designed to establish whether vaccination has measurable benefits against Bundibugyo virus disease and to gather the safety and immunogenicity evidence needed to interpret any protection signal. Ervebo is expected to be the first vaccine tested. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, or CEPI, said Oct. 13 that two vaccines tailored to Bundibugyo virus were also in early-stage studies: an mRNA candidate from Moderna and a ChAdOx1 candidate developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India. Those candidates could be added to Tumaini when available. How Tumaini is designed to work CEPI’s description of Tumaini calls it a pivotal Phase 2/3 adaptive platform trial. Rather than creating a separate full trial for every product, a platform can assess more than one candidate under a shared framework as new vaccines become ready for study. Tumaini uses ring vaccination, directing study vaccination toward people at high risk after an identified exposure. The study uses a ring-vaccination approach, focusing on contacts considered at high risk of infection. Such rings can include people exposed to a person with confirmed illness and others with close connections to that exposure. The approach directs study activity toward people most likely to encounter the virus, which can be especially important when cases are geographically clustered. CEPI says the trial is intended to assess safety, immunogenicity—the body’s immune response—and efficacy, or whether vaccination reduces disease among people at risk. But the public descriptions do not give a planned sample size, detailed endpoint definitions, statistical analysis plan or the trial’s allocation and comparator arrangements. Those omissions make it too early to infer how quickly a reliable efficacy answer may emerge. News reports say Tumaini will include pregnant women and children 12 and older. Detailed eligibility criteria have not been published in the material describing the launch. The trial is led by the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale and the University of Antwerp’s Global Health Institute, with the Congolese Ministry of Health serving as national lead. CEPI identifies the two research institutions as co-sponsors; WHO is providing strategic, technical and scientific advice rather than sponsoring the study. A vaccine study, separate from the treatment trial Tumaini follows another clinical study in the country, but the two trials address different questions. In July, WHO announced enrollment in PARTNERS, a randomized therapeutic trial for people already confirmed to have Bundibugyo virus disease. That study is evaluating the experimental antibody treatment MBP134 and the antiviral remdesivir. The WHO announcement of PARTNERS described a search for treatments that could improve outcomes after infection. Tumaini, by contrast, is testing prevention among people at heightened risk of exposure. A favorable result in one study would not establish that the intervention in the other works. Outbreak totals have varied in public accounts over the course of the year, with reports citing different dates and case definitions. The important point for Tumaini’s scientific purpose is that an active outbreak can provide the exposures needed to assess whether a vaccine changes disease risk. It can also complicate the work: transmission patterns, access to affected communities and the pace of case detection may all affect how much evidence accumulates. What evidence the trial could provide A Phase 2/3 label does not mean a vaccine has been shown to work. Phase 2 research commonly examines safety and immune responses, while Phase 3 evidence is typically used to assess whether an intervention prevents disease. Tumaini’s adaptive structure is intended to move candidates through those questions in an outbreak setting, but its results will depend on the number and timing of infections observed during the study. For Ervebo, the trial may clarify whether an immune response developed for Zaire ebolavirus has useful cross-protection against Bundibugyo virus. For the newer candidates, it could provide a route to compare products designed specifically for the circulating virus. Neither possibility is a result yet. The first vaccinations therefore mark the beginning of evidence gathering, not a change in the regulatory status of any vaccine for Bundibugyo virus disease. The study’s eventual value will rest on the outcome data it produces: whether vaccinated high-risk participants show protection, how durable any protection is, and whether the safety findings support use in the populations enrolled. ByPam Belluck Pam Belluck is a seasoned health and science journalist whose work explores the impact of medicine, policy, and innovation on individuals and society. She has reported extensively on topics like reproductive health, long-term illness, brain science, and public health, with a focus on both complex medical developments and human-centered narratives. Her writing bridges investigative depth with accessible storytelling, often covering issues at the intersection of science, ethics, and personal experience. Pam continues to examine the evolving challenges in health and medicine across global and local contexts. selected_identity.page_title: Tumaini Trial Begins Vaccinating Participants in DR Congo

news.content_original: News Technology Business Entertainment Science & Health Knowledge Base Font ResizerAa Search News Technology Business Entertainment Science & Health Knowledge Base Follow US Tumaini Trial Begins Vaccinating Participants in DR Congo Last updated: October 25, 2026 12:36 am By Pam Belluck Science & Health 7 Min Read SHARE First participants in the Tumaini vaccine trial have reportedly been vaccinated in Bunia, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province, opening a study meant to answer a still-unresolved question: whether an existing Ebola vaccine can protect people against Bundibugyo virus disease. Several reports published Oct. 24 said the first volunteers received Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. The launch, reported by Al Jazeera and corroborated by MedicalXpress in an AFP report, is a research milestone during an active outbreak, not evidence that the vaccine works against Bundibugyo virus. No safety, immune-response or efficacy results from Tumaini have been released. Table of Contents Why Ervebo is being studied How Tumaini is designed to work A vaccine study, separate from the treatment trial What evidence the trial could provide Why Ervebo is being studied Bundibugyo virus is distinct from Zaire ebolavirus, even though both are among the viruses that can cause Ebola disease. A vaccine’s protection against one virus cannot be assumed to extend to another; cross-protection has to be demonstrated in study results. In May, a World Health Organization expert review said no vaccine or treatment had been specifically approved for Bundibugyo virus disease. It described the evidence that Ervebo might protect against Bundibugyo virus as limited and inconclusive, and advised that its use for that purpose be evaluated in carefully designed research. That is the purpose of Tumaini, whose name means “hope” in Swahili. The trial is not a routine outbreak vaccination campaign. It is designed to establish whether vaccination has measurable benefits against Bundibugyo virus disease and to gather the safety and immunogenicity evidence needed to interpret any protection signal. Ervebo is expected to be the first vaccine tested. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, or CEPI, said Oct. 13 that two vaccines tailored to Bundibugyo virus were also in early-stage studies: an mRNA candidate from Moderna and a ChAdOx1 candidate developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India. Those candidates could be added to Tumaini when available. How Tumaini is designed to work CEPI’s description of Tumaini calls it a pivotal Phase 2/3 adaptive platform trial. Rather than creating a separate full trial for every product, a platform can assess more than one candidate under a shared framework as new vaccines become ready for study. Tumaini uses ring vaccination, directing study vaccination toward people at high risk after an identified exposure. The study uses a ring-vaccination approach, focusing on contacts considered at high risk of infection. Such rings can include people exposed to a person with confirmed illness and others with close connections to that exposure. The approach directs study activity toward people most likely to encounter the virus, which can be especially important when cases are geographically clustered. CEPI says the trial is intended to assess safety, immunogenicity—the body’s immune response—and efficacy, or whether vaccination reduces disease among people at risk. But the public descriptions do not give a planned sample size, detailed endpoint definitions, statistical analysis plan or the trial’s allocation and comparator arrangements. Those omissions make it too early to infer how quickly a reliable efficacy answer may emerge. News reports say Tumaini will include pregnant women and children 12 and older. Detailed eligibility criteria have not been published in the material describing the launch. The trial is led by the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale and the University of Antwerp’s Global Health Institute, with the Congolese Ministry of Health serving as national lead. CEPI identifies the two research institutions as co-sponsors; WHO is providing strategic, technical and scientific advice rather than sponsoring the study. A vaccine study, separate from the treatment trial Tumaini follows another clinical study in the country, but the two trials address different questions. In July, WHO announced enrollment in PARTNERS, a randomized therapeutic trial for people already confirmed to have Bundibugyo virus disease. That study is evaluating the experimental antibody treatment MBP134 and the antiviral remdesivir. The WHO announcement of PARTNERS described a search for treatments that could improve outcomes after infection. Tumaini, by contrast, is testing prevention among people at heightened risk of exposure. A favorable result in one study would not establish that the intervention in the other works. Outbreak totals have varied in public accounts over the course of the year, with reports citing different dates and case definitions. The important point for Tumaini’s scientific purpose is that an active outbreak can provide the exposures needed to assess whether a vaccine changes disease risk. It can also complicate the work: transmission patterns, access to affected communities and the pace of case detection may all affect how much evidence accumulates. What evidence the trial could provide A Phase 2/3 label does not mean a vaccine has been shown to work. Phase 2 research commonly examines safety and immune responses, while Phase 3 evidence is typically used to assess whether an intervention prevents disease. Tumaini’s adaptive structure is intended to move candidates through those questions in an outbreak setting, but its results will depend on the number and timing of infections observed during the study. For Ervebo, the trial may clarify whether an immune response developed for Zaire ebolavirus has useful cross-protection against Bundibugyo virus. For the newer candidates, it could provide a route to compare products designed specifically for the circulating virus. Neither possibility is a result yet. The first vaccinations therefore mark the beginning of evidence gathering, not a change in the regulatory status of any vaccine for Bundibugyo virus disease. The study’s eventual value will rest on the outcome data it produces: whether vaccinated high-risk participants show protection, how durable any protection is, and whether the safety findings support use in the populations enrolled. ByPam Belluck Pam Belluck is a seasoned health and science journalist whose work explores the impact of medicine, policy, and innovation on individuals and society. She has reported extensively on topics like reproductive health, long-term illness, brain science, and public health, with a focus on both complex medical developments and human-centered narratives. Her writing bridges investigative depth with accessible storytelling, often covering issues at the intersection of science, ethics, and personal experience. Pam continues to examine the evolving challenges in health and medicine across global and local contexts. news.content_title: First participant vaccinated in pivotal Phase 2/3 Bundibugyo vaccine trial in DRC
news.content: Securing the future: CEPI's 3.0 Investment Case Find out moreDismiss About What we do Partner with us Our impact News & stories Contact us News First participant vaccinated in pivotal Phase 2/3 Bundibugyo vaccine trial in DRC 23rd October 2026 Share Tumaini, a pivotal Phase 2/3 clinical trial, will evaluate vaccine candidates including Ervebo as part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) outbreak response. There is currently no approved vaccine against Bundibugyo virus. Tumaini aims to close that gap by generating robust evidence about the performance of multiple vaccine candidates. BUNIA, DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO, 23 October 2026 – The first participant has been vaccinated in Tumaini, a pivotal Phase 2/3 clinical trial of vaccine candidates against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). The vaccination, administered on 23 October 2026 in Bunia, DRC marks the start of the trial, which will support the Government-led response to the ongoing outbreak. The trial begins as the DRC faces the largest recorded BDBV outbreak and the second-largest Ebola outbreak to date. The outbreak was officially declared on 15 May 2026 and was determined as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization (WHO) and a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security by Africa CDC in the days thereafter. As of 21 October 2026, 9,552 cases and 4,602 deaths had been confirmed in the DRC [1]. There is currently no approved vaccine to protect against BDBV. Tumaini, which means “hope” in Swahili, aims to close that gap by evaluating the safety, immunogenicity and efficacy of vaccine candidates, including Ervebo which is currently licensed for use to prevent Ebola virus (EBOV). Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future BDBV outbreaks. Prof. Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, Incident Manager of the Ebola Response, Democratic Republic of the Congo, said: “Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities. Our priority is to stop transmission and save lives, while ensuring that research is closely coordinated with frontline response activities. We thank the participants, communities and partners whose trust and engagement make it possible to evaluate potential new tools against Bundibugyo virus.” Tumaini is an adaptive platform trial, which allows several vaccine candidates to be evaluated in parallel within a single framework and saves valuable time during an outbreak. Candidates will be assessed through ring vaccination, which focuses on contacts at high risk of infection. Technical details are available on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07842107). Vaccine candidates are selected through an independent prioritisation process led by the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritisation (TAG-CVP), and corresponding protocol amendments are approved by ACOREP, the national regulatory authority. The first candidate to enter the trial is Ervebo. Preparations are underway for two CEPI-funded BDBV-specific vaccine candidates, under development by Moderna and by the University of Oxford in collaboration with Serum Institute of India, to enter the trial shortly. The Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) and the University of Antwerp (Global Health Institute) co-lead and co-sponsor the trial. The DRC Ministry of Health provides national leadership and oversight. A Trial Steering Committee, chaired by the Ministry’s Incident Response Manager, provides strategic oversight and aligns the trial with the wider outbreak response and with other studies of medical countermeasures in the region. Prof. Hugo Kavunga, Tumaini Co-Sponsor and Principal Investigator, Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale, said: “Vaccinating the first participant is an important milestone, made possible by the dedication of Congolese researchers, health workers and our partners. With affected communities at the heart of this effort, we are placing national scientific leadership at the service of the outbreak response. Our priority is to establish which vaccines can safely and effectively protect those at risk.” Prof. Jean-Pierre Van geertruyden, Tumaini Co-Sponsor and Co-Principal Investigator, University of Antwerp, said: “During an outbreak, speed and scientific rigour must go hand in hand. Tumaini brings together Congolese and international expertise to generate reliable evidence on vaccines against Bundibugyo virus. Through this partnership, we aim to support the response today while building the knowledge needed to protect communities in future outbreaks.” Africa CDC plays a strategic role in advancing African-led clinical research, strengthening regional coordination, ensuring that emerging scientific evidence informs public health decision-making and the wider Ebola outbreak response, and supporting timely and equitable access to successful vaccine candidates. Through the R&D Blueprint, WHO has developed protocols for filovirus vaccine studies that were adapted rapidly for the Tumaini trial. WHO provides leadership in the BVD response supporting the Ministry of Health of the DRC. For the Tumaini trial, WHO provides strategic, technical and scientific advice along with on-the-ground experience to stand up a vaccine trial embedded in an emergency response. CEPI provides funding, scientific expertise and operational support and is backing a portfolio of BDBV-specific vaccine candidates that could be evaluated in the study. Partners including Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the Institute of Tropical Medicine Antwerp (ITM), WHO and Africa CDC support implementation of the trial. MSF uses the organisation’s own funding and operational capacity to support the trial. Tumaini is funded by CEPI’s Bundibugyo virus vaccine development programme, which, to date, is backed by the European Commission, the U.S. Department of State, the Fund for Science and Technology, the Republic of Korea and CEPI’s core funding. Beyond the trial, Tumaini is part of a broader “push–pull” partnership between CEPI and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, in which Gavi has committed up to US$40 million to fund manufacturing readiness to ensure vaccines are available at scale as soon as they are approved for deployment. Dr Richard Hatchett, CEO of CEPI, said: “There is still no licensed vaccine against Bundibugyo virus, and the cost of that absence is being counted in the DRC every day, in lives lost and in health workers who go to work without protection. Tumaini aims to change that. Today’s first vaccination opens a pivotal trial to generate the evidence needed to get safe and effective vaccines to the people who need them most.” Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, Executive Director, Health Emergencies Programme, World Health Organization, said: "The launch of the Tumaini trial marks a critical step towards establishing whether candidate vaccines can effectively protect people against the Bundibugyo virus. This is much more than a research study. The trial reflects WHO’s strong recommendation to evaluate candidate vaccines through well-designed research during outbreaks, using a single adaptive platform and a ring vaccination approach. This is an approach WHO and countries have used in previous outbreaks to test vaccines, including the one that is effective against Ebola virus (previously known as Zaire ebolavirus). The trial is an opportunity to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether these vaccines can protect people at risk. If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus, a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives." Prof. Placide Mbala, Director of Research, Clinical Trials and Innovation at Africa CDC, said : “Tumaini means hope, and today that hope is being translated into action. At a time when our communities are facing the largest recorded Bundibugyo outbreak, this trial demonstrates the power of African-led research to address African public health challenges. This is our collective commitment to generating high-quality evidence that can save lives today while strengthening preparedness for future epidemics.” Prof. Wim Adriaensen, Head of the Clinical Immunology Unit at ITM, said: “Through the long-standing partnership between INRB and ITM, we can quickly bring the required laboratory capacity to the affected region. This helps us identify the immune responses associated with vaccine protection. We can then compare vaccines that arrive late in, or even after, the outbreak with those protective immune responses, so promising candidates aren’t overlooked simply because they become available at a later stage.” Valérie Briand, Head of the Research Department, Epicentre, said: “Children are among those hardest hit by the Ebola outbreak in certain regions, yet they have historically been under-represented in clinical research. The inclusion of pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, as well as children from one year of age for the Ervebo vaccine, represents an important step towards generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials. Discussions are already ongoing to extend inclusion to younger children for specific vaccine candidates.” Bern-Thomas Nyang'wa, Medical Director, MSF, said: “The Tumaini trial represents a critical step towards addressing the urgent needs of people most affected by Bundibugyo virus. MSF brings to this trial its experience of doing clinical research in close collaboration with affected communities. Working in partnership with communities is essential for building trust and ensuring meaningful participation in the development of vaccines that are effective, adapted, and accessible to those who need them most.” [1] DRC Ebola Bundibugyo - Epidemic Intelligence Dashboard This press release is also available in French. Ebola is rapidly spreading across multiple countries in Africa. AFP via Getty Images The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) reported 10,000 confirmed cases of Ebola this week, with nearly 4000+ deaths. Health officials are now concerned that numbers may soon reach a point of inflection where cross-border spread and rampant infection throughout the continent may become impossible to contain. Other countries, including Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have also reported numerous cases in recent weeks. Public health officials both at the global level and national front are rushing to mobilize care for those affected in addition to public health resources to help manage the rapid spread of the disease. This week, the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also provided an update regarding the evolving situation: "This outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.... [and] The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region." Some of the complexities the agency cites include challenges in health infrastructure and access to care locally, ongoing violence and conflict across certain regions, and consistent lack of trust in public health initiatives. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Governments including the United States have also issued strict quarantine and return to home guidelines for travelers: "All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane." The World Health Organization explains that Ebola symptoms can be somewhat elusive and easily confused for other common ailments; standard symptoms include "fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat...vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, internal and external bleeding etc." It also explains that timelines and testing are important aspects of confirmatory diagnosis: "The time interval from infection to onset of symptoms ranges from 2 to 21 days....Even when people have developed Ebola disease-like symptoms, only a laboratory test can confirm whether the cause is Ebola." Unfortunately, treatment options are typically limited and Ebola is notorious for high mortality rates. The best way for patients to be safe is to ensure that they do not expose themselves to the virus or to people that may be transmitting the virus. Although Ebola breakouts by no means are new, this is a rapidly evolving situation that requires close attention from the international public heath community. news.title_original: Congo Reports Over 10,000 Ebola Cases, Sparking Concerns of Wider Spread

analysis.time: The outbreak was reported as of October 27, 2026, with the DRC reporting 10,000 confirmed cases this week. The time interval from infection to onset of symptoms ranges from 2 to 21 days (N6, N14).
analysis.location_and_population: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is the primary location, with cases also reported in Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda (N6, N8).
analysis.event: The DRC reported 10,000 confirmed cases of Ebola virus disease, with nearly 4,000 deaths, sparking concerns about wider spread (N6).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has reached 10,000 confirmed cases and nearly 4,000 deaths, with health officials concerned about cross-border spread and containment challenges (N6, N7, N11).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials are mobilizing care and resources to manage the spread, and the CDC has issued quarantine guidelines for travelers from the DRC. However, the situation remains under investigation due to challenges in health infrastructure, access to care, and local trust (N9, N10, N11, N13).

analysis.brief_en: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reported over 10,000 confirmed cases of Ebola virus disease, with nearly 4,000 deaths, raising concerns about the potential for wider spread across Africa. Health officials are worried that the outbreak may reach a critical point where cross-border transmission becomes difficult to contain. Countries like Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda have also reported numerous cases in recent weeks, indicating the disease's growing reach. The World Health Organization notes that Ebola symptoms can be mistaken for other illnesses, and only laboratory testing can confirm the diagnosis. The CDC has issued quarantine guidelines for U.S. nationals who have been in the DRC, requiring them to stay outside the country for 21 days before entering the United States. Challenges such as weak health infrastructure, limited access to care, and local distrust in public health initiatives are complicating the response. Despite these difficulties, global and national health authorities are working to mobilize resources and manage the outbreak. The situation remains under investigation, with the potential for further escalation.
analysis.summary_en: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reported over 10,000 confirmed cases of Ebola virus disease, with nearly 4,000 deaths, raising concerns about the potential for wider spread across Africa. Health officials are worried that the outbreak may reach a critical point where cross-border transmission becomes difficult to contain. Countries like Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda have also reported numerous cases in recent weeks, indicating the disease's growing reach. Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in more than a decade became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country. The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added. The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history. The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public. The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation. Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country. Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere. Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.” The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said. Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission. “What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said. Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding. The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them. The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only globally to the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000. Officials emphasize the need for rapid response and cross-border collaboration to prevent further spread, as the situation remains uncertain and under investigation.

supplementary_news.content_title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow the spread in African countries
supplementary_news.content: A medical worker checks a patient at an Ebola treatment center in Bunia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, on Oct. 18. Xinhua News Agency / via Getty Oct. 27, 2026, 9:23 AM UTC / Source : The Associated Press By The Associated Press The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reached 10,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Tuesday, as health authorities race to slow the spread of the disease in multiple African countries. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, and nearly half of the 10,060 confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo’s Ministry of Health. That also makes it the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the country’s history. The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation. Those obstacles compound the challenge of persuading people to report symptoms and accept care in communities that have endured years of violence and repeated epidemics. Compared with the West Africa Ebola outbreak of 2014-16 — history’s largest and deadliest with more than 28,000 cases, including over 11,000 deaths — this has had at least three times the number of cases and number of deaths in the time since it was declared. It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions with cases recorded in Kenya and Nigeria as well. It has so far been recorded in five countries, including Uganda and France, both of which have no active cases at the moment. A recurring problem in the spread in Africa is what appears to be lax surveillance efforts, as most of the first cases were confirmed long after people started showing symptoms or after traveling. In Congo, the disease has spread to 66 health zones across eight provinces, from three zones when it was first declared in May. Responders have told The Associated Press that they’re seeing treatment centers in some of those health zones getting overwhelmed, with people still skeptical and violent toward them, and that health workers are regularly going on strike to protest delayed or unpaid wages. A medical worker patrols an Ebola treatment center in Bunia on Oct. 18. Xinhua News Agency via Getty “Some people still don’t seem to understand the seriousness of the situation even though they are directly exposed to the risk,” said Sephora Bgosi with the Ebola burial team in Ituri province, the epicenter. “Ebola disease is extremely dangerous and can be deadly,” said Bgosi. About 80% of recorded cases are still coming from outside monitored contacts, showing there are ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of. At least 95% of recorded cases are supposed to be coming from known contacts for officials to say the outbreak has largely been brought under control, the Africa CDC has said. At least half of deaths recorded are among people who have not been admitted to treatment centers, a sign that people are still not reporting symptoms at all in many areas. In many zones, health workers are battling challenges ranging from basic needs such as adequate vehicles to complex ones like persuading families to release their relatives who are sick with the disease or who have died from it and need to be buried safely. Last week at the Nia Nia health zone in Ituri province, some Ebola responders, including surveillance and community engagement officers, went on strike over unpaid bonuses owed since late August, a common trend across many affected localities. More than five months since the outbreak was declared, health workers are still being attacked by angry villagers, including on Saturday when a nurse was killed and another health worker severely injured while responding to an Ebola alert in Bafwasende, Tshopo province. The outbreak has disrupted essential health services that are already underfunded and overstretched and has shifted attention away from other disease outbreaks the country is battling, such as cholera. More pregnant women are dying as they avoid hospitals over fear of infection and isolation, causing maternal mortality to double in some provinces soon after the outbreak was declared. RSS feeds → Contact → Sign in Editors' picks | Epidemics | Mass death Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak passes 10 000 confirmed cases in DRC ByRishav Kothari Tuesday, October 27, 2026 18:15 UTCTuesday, October 27, 2026 18:16 UTC Follow us on Google News The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reached 10 060 confirmed cases and 4 887 confirmed deaths as of October 25, 2026, according to the country’s public health institute. Its situation report, published on October 26, recorded cases across 66 health zones in eight provinces. Image credit: ECDC Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo recorded 10 060 confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola cases and 4 887 confirmed deaths through October 25, 2026. A government report, published on October 26, also showed contact monitoring below the response target, with data available from five provinces. The report recorded 96 newly notified cases and 46 deaths as of October 25, including 40 community deaths and six in treatment centers. It listed 2 684 recoveries and a cumulative case-fatality ratio of 48.6%. Nord Kivu had 2 309 cases and 1 293 deaths, Haut-Uélé 436 cases and 190 deaths, and Tshopo 83 cases and 27 deaths. The other affected provinces were Bas-Uélé, Sud Kivu, Sud-Ubangi and Nord-Ubangi. Distribution of cumulative confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of October 20, 2026. Credit: WHO Contact monitoring remained below the 95% response target. Across the five provinces submitting contact-follow-up data for October 25, teams saw 16 205 of 19 853 listed contacts during the preceding 24 hours, a rate of 81.6%. This was not a complete measure for every affected province. The government report said that attacks and threats against response teams, including the killing of a nurse, had prevented Bafwasende health zone in Tshopo from submitting data. The World Health Organization (WHO) described transmission as sustained and high-level in its October 23 assessment. Its data through October 20 showed that 50 of 66 affected health zones had reported at least one new case during the preceding 21 days; the other 16 had reported no recent cases. Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by date of notification, as of October 20, 2026. Credit: WHO Number of deaths among confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by date of notification, as of October 20, 2026. Credit: WHO In Kenya, WHO reported nine confirmed cases and two deaths as of October 26. All nine belonged to one connected cluster, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Twenty contacts were released from quarantine after completing 21 days without symptoms, while 98 remained in quarantine. Nigeria confirmed its imported case in Abuja on October 20. The Nigeria Center for Disease Control and Prevention listed 53 contacts in its October 24 situation report, replacing the earlier count of 44. Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in Kenya, by date of notification, as of October 21, 2026. Credit: WHO Swiss authorities said the patient was evacuated from Nigeria to Geneva on October 26 and was in stable condition. Her husband was isolated in Zurich as a close contact. He was not reported as a second confirmed case. Investigations into the patient’s source of infection continued. WHO’s October 23 update listed cases in five countries since the outbreak was declared on May 15: the DRC, Uganda, France, Kenya and Nigeria. Map of parts of DRC affected by Ebola Bundibugyo Virus outbreak in 2026. Credit: ECDC No approved vaccine or specific treatment is available for Bundibugyo virus disease. On October 23, researchers in Bunia vaccinated the first participant in the TUMAINI Phase 2/3 trial, which evaluates candidate vaccines including Ervebo. Ervebo is licensed against a different Ebola virus; its use in the trial does not establish protection against Bundibugyo. WHO’s October 23 report still cited its August 14 risk assessment: very high in the DRC, high in countries sharing its land borders, and low for the rest of the African Region and globally. WHO said that assessment was being revised and continued to advise against general travel or trade restrictions. Bundibugyo virus spreads through direct contact with infected blood or other bodily fluids, or contaminated materials. Symptoms can appear two to 21 days after infection, and people do not transmit the disease before symptoms begin. Early supportive care can improve survival. WHO classifies the epidemic as the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the DRC, irrespective of virus species.
